```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
library(plotly)
s <- jsonlite::fromJSON("results/summary.json")
monthly <- read.csv("results/tables/monthly.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
monthly$date <- as.Date(monthly$date)
series <- read.csv("config/series.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
source("R/figure.R")
f <- function(x) sprintf("%.1f", x)
value <- function(label, column = "cumulative_pct") {
  result <- s$series[[column]][s$series$label == label]
  stopifnot(length(result) == 1L, is.finite(result))
  result
}
```

In December 2024, the grocery price index was `r f(value("Groceries"))`% above December 2019. Applying that average increase to a \$100 grocery bill gives about \$`r sprintf("%.0f", 100 + value("Groceries"))`. Yet grocery inflation over the final twelve months was only `r f(value("Groceries", "annual_pct"))`%. A slower rate did not bring prices back to their earlier level.

This post asks a concrete historical question: **which of five everyday spending categories was furthest above its pre-pandemic price level by December 2024?** I compare groceries, rent, electricity, gasoline, and clothing with December 2019. They are selected examples, not a complete household budget. The overall Consumer Price Index, or CPI, provides a benchmark.

The answer depends on which change we look at. Overall prices were `r f(value("Overall CPI"))`% above December 2019, even though inflation over the final twelve months was `r f(value("Overall CPI", "annual_pct"))`%. Both figures describe the same December 2024 price index. They simply answer questions over different time spans.

## Explore the difference

The chart opens with each category's percentage change since December 2019. Zero means its price index is back at that starting level. Use the menu to switch to **Year-over-year**, which compares each month with the same month one year earlier.

Try one comparison: double-click **Groceries** in the legend to isolate it, then switch views and hover over August 2022 and December 2024. Double-click its legend entry again to restore the other categories.

```{r}
#| label: fig-price-explorer
#| fig-cap: "One chart, two comparisons: cumulative price increases since December 2019 and changes from twelve months earlier. Monthly U.S. CPI-U indexes, not seasonally adjusted, through December 2024. Source: BLS via FRED."
#| fig-alt: "Interactive lines for five selected spending categories and overall CPI, with a cumulative-change or annual-inflation selector and category legend controls."
#| out-width: "100%"
make_price_figure(monthly, series)
```

## The largest increase was electricity

By December 2024, electricity's index was `r f(value("Electricity"))`% above its December 2019 level, the largest increase among these five categories. Groceries followed at `r f(value("Groceries"))`%, with rent close behind at `r f(value("Rent"))`%. Each had risen more than the overall CPI benchmark.

Gasoline was up `r f(value("Gasoline"))`%, while clothing was up `r f(value("Clothing"))`%. A budget concentrated in electricity and groceries, with little spent on clothing, could have risen faster than the `r f(value("Overall CPI"))`% overall figure. A household's actual increase depends on its full spending mix; these indexes do not measure a particular family's bills.

The ranking is tied to the dates. Electricity also had the largest increase at the end of 2023, but gasoline then ranked above rent. By the end of 2024, those two had switched places. Moving the endpoint can change the comparison, which is one reason to explore the path instead of reading only the final values.

## A slower rate can still leave a higher price

With groceries isolated, switch between views for `r format(as.Date(s$grocery_peak_inflation_date), "%B %Y")` and December 2024. Their annual inflation rate fell from `r f(s$grocery_peak_inflation_pct)`% to `r f(value("Groceries", "annual_pct"))`%, yet the grocery price index rose another `r f(s$grocery_change_after_peak_inflation_pct)`% between those dates. Switching views shows how a falling inflation rate can coexist with a rising price level.

Gasoline illustrates a different outcome. In December 2024, its index was `r f(abs(value("Gasoline", "annual_pct")))`% below December 2023. Prices had actually fallen over that year. Switch back to the cumulative view, though, and gasoline remained `r f(value("Gasoline"))`% above December 2019. A recent decline did not reverse the full earlier increase.

## What this comparison can tell us

The [Bureau of Labor Statistics](https://www.bls.gov/cpi/questions-and-answers.htm) measures price changes for urban consumers. These national indexes do not describe a particular store, city, or shopping list. The [rent index](https://www.bls.gov/cpi/factsheets/owners-equivalent-rent-and-rent.htm) covers rents paid for occupied homes, including continuing tenants, rather than only newly advertised apartments. The data are not seasonally adjusted; December-to-December comparisons keep the endpoint months consistent, while shorter movements can reflect seasonal patterns.

This is a historical price comparison, not a report on today's prices. It contains no earnings data, so it cannot establish whether households became better or worse off. Nor can the lines identify which policies or market forces caused the changes.

The main takeaways are:

* Electricity, groceries, and rent rose more than overall CPI in this five-year comparison.
* Slower grocery inflation left the earlier price increase largely intact.
* Gasoline fell during 2024 but remained above its 2019 starting point. Always specify the comparison dates.

**Data and replication:** BLS CPI-U series distributed by [FRED](https://fred.stlouisfed.org/). Exact series, sources, limitations, and instructions are in the [GitHub repository](https://github.com/yipin-grena/aeds6400-blog/tree/main/posts/everyday-prices).
